summaries.example: Imagine two children looking at a table. One says, “There is a table.” Another says, “There are only many tiny pieces arranged table-like.” They may disagree about what exists. A philosopher who studies whether this disagreement is a deep question, a word problem, or not a question with a true answer is studying metaphysics at a higher level.
summaries.summary: This entry is about a debate over metaphysics itself. Metaphysics asks broad questions such as whether tables, numbers, or past things exist. Realists about metaphysics say these can be important questions about reality. Anti-realists say that some such questions go wrong. They may say a question is trivial, meaning its answer follows from word meanings or simple facts; merely verbal, meaning people are using language differently; or non-factual, meaning there is no fact that makes either answer true. The entry also describes objections to these views. Critics ask whether one meaning of “exists” is better than others, whether anti-realists secretly accept a strong view about what exists, and whether the proposed languages really matter. Some broader views say science should provide the needed answers, while others treat many existence questions as easy or without definite answers.
key_ideas: The entry separates questions about reality from questions about whether a metaphysical question is a good, deep question.
Anti-realists criticize particular questions, such as whether tables or numbers exist.
Three local criticisms are trivialism, mere-verbalism, and non-factualism.
Realists reply that metaphysical questions may concern reality itself, not just language.
Some philosophers offer wider criticisms, saying science should guide or replace much metaphysics.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often argue about whether something is real, possible, or important. Before trying to settle the argument, it helps to ask what kind of disagreement it is. This topic teaches us to notice the difference between disagreeing about the world and disagreeing about words. It also shows why philosophers examine the rules and assumptions behind a question, not only its possible answers.

important_terms.definition: The study of very general questions about what is real and what kinds of things exist.
A view that a metaphysical question asks about an important part of reality, not merely about words.
A view that something is wrong with a particular metaphysical question.
The idea that a question has an answer, but the answer is easy and based mostly on meanings or ordinary facts.
The idea that a disagreement may come only from people using a word in different ways.
The idea that there is no true answer to a particular question.

questions_to_think_about: If people use the same word differently, are they really disagreeing?
Is the question “Do tables exist?” deep, easy, or unclear?
Can a question have no true answer?
When should science help answer a question about reality?

summaries.example: Consider the sentence “There are tables.” A realist about the composite-object question may regard it as a substantive claim about mind-independent reality. A trivialist may say that the existence of objects arranged tablewise, together with the meaning of “table,” already settles it. A mere-verbalist may say that rival philosophers use different quantifier meanings, so their dispute is merely verbal. A non-factualist may instead say that the relevant sentence lacks a determinate truth value. These positions concern the status of the question, not simply which answer about tables is correct.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys metametaphysical debates about whether metaphysical questions are genuine and substantive. It begins by separating realism about metaphysics from realism within metaphysics. For example, believing that tables exist is a first-order metaphysical position; believing that the question of whether tables exist is deep and fact-based is a second-order position. Local anti-realists challenge particular questions in three main ways. Trivialists hold that a question has an answer but that it is settled by meanings and ordinary facts. Mere-verbalists hold that apparent opponents speak different languages, so no non-verbal dispute remains. Non-factualists hold that there is no fact of the matter, perhaps because the relevant language is too imprecise or because nothing determines reference or truth. These positions can overlap. The entry then presents realist objections: perhaps one meaning of “exists” is privileged by the best theory of reality; perhaps accepting truth in one language leads to an overly expansive ontology; perhaps trivialist semantics cannot preserve ordinary compositional meaning; and perhaps substantialist languages are the ones relevant to the questions philosophers actually intend. It also discusses global anti-realist proposals based on science, broad trivialism, or neo-positivism, while noting continuing questions about self-refutation and the status of anti-metaphysical theories themselves.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes realism and anti-realism about metaphysical questions from realism and anti-realism within metaphysics. A person can be realist about tables yet anti-realist about whether the table question is deep.
Local anti-realism includes trivialism, mere-verbalism, and non-factualism. These views criticize particular questions rather than metaphysics as a whole.
Mere-verbalism can involve rival languages in which the same sentence is obviously true in one and obviously false in another.

Non-factualism may arise because relevant sentences are imprecise, because nothing fixes reference, because a disputed quantifier is defective, or because a question presupposes facts that do not exist.
Realist objections appeal to metaphysical privilege, the threat of maximalism, problems with analyticity and compositional meaning, and the difficulty of identifying the rival languages.
Global views include science-centered anti-metaphysical positions, general trivialism, and neo-positivism; the entry notes that newer views address self-refutation worries differently.
summaries.why_it_matters: Metaphysical arguments can appear to disagree while actually operating with different assumptions about language, truth, and reality. Understanding these levels of disagreement helps students evaluate arguments more carefully. The debate also raises a general philosophical issue: when a question seems confused or unanswerable, should we revise the question, revise our language, or conclude that reality supplies no answer?

important_terms.definition: The study of fundamental questions about what exists, what reality is like, and how its basic features are related.
A view about whether a metaphysical question is a genuine, substantive question about mind-independent reality.
A local anti-realist view that a question has an answer, but its answer follows trivially from semantic facts and uncontroversial empirical facts.
A view that a dispute is produced by different meanings or languages, rather than by disagreement about the non-linguistic world.
A view that no answer to a question is true because there is no fact of the matter.
A language in which an existence claim requires a further, metaphysically substantial fact beyond a pattern of ordinary objects or simples.
A view that different speakers or communities use quantifiers such as “exists” with different meanings.
A debate about how a term should be used, rather than a debate about what the world is independently like.

questions_to_think_about: Does a disagreement become merely verbal whenever speakers attach different meanings to a sentence?
What would make one interpretation of “exists” metaphysically privileged?
Can a sentence be meaningful yet fail to have a determinate truth value?
If a language makes an existence claim trivially true, does that show that the objects exist in a substantive sense?
Should the success of science limit the questions metaphysics may ask?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya says, “That drink is a martini,” because it is in a V-shaped glass. Leo says it is not, because he thinks a martini must contain gin and vermouth. If they agree on what is in the glass and disagree only about the word “martini,” their debate may be merely verbal. Philosophers ask whether some arguments about tables, numbers, or time work in the same way—or whether those arguments are really about reality.
summaries.summary: This entry examines a debate about metaphysics at a higher level: not simply what exists, but whether metaphysical questions are genuine questions about reality. It distinguishes this from ordinary metaphysical disputes. For instance, a person who says tables exist is taking a position within metaphysics. Someone who says that the question “Do tables exist?” is trivial, merely verbal, or non-factual is taking a position about metaphysics itself. The entry focuses mostly on local criticisms of particular questions. Trivialism says that a question has an answer, but the answer follows from meanings or easy facts. Mere-verbalism says that opposing speakers use different languages, making their dispute about words rather than the world. Non-factualism says that there is no true answer, perhaps because the important terms are too unclear or because nothing makes one answer correct. Realist responses challenge these ideas. They ask whether reality favors one meaning of “exists,” whether anti-realism accidentally supports an extremely crowded picture of reality, and whether the proposed languages are really the ones relevant to the debate. The entry also describes more global approaches, including science-centered criticisms, general trivialism, and neo-positivism.
key_ideas: The entry studies realism and anti-realism about metaphysics, not mainly whether particular things such as tables exist.
A philosopher could believe that tables exist but still think the question of whether tables exist is trivial or merely verbal.
Trivialists, mere-verbalists, and non-factualists give different explanations of what goes wrong with some metaphysical questions.
A merely verbal debate involves different meanings and answers that are obvious within the speakers’ different languages.
Realists object that metaphysical questions may concern reality itself and that anti-realists may not have identified convincing rival languages.
The entry also considers broader anti-metaphysical views, including views that give science a central role.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many disagreements become clearer when we separate three questions: What is the world like? What do our words mean? And is this a meaningful question to ask? This distinction is useful in philosophy and in everyday arguments. It encourages careful listening, prevents people from treating every disagreement as the same kind of disagreement, and shows why philosophers sometimes debate the assumptions behind a question.

important_terms.definition: The study of broad questions about what exists and what reality is like.
The position that a particular metaphysical question is a real and important question about the world.
The position that a particular metaphysical question is defective or misleading in some way.
The view that a question has an answer, but the answer is obvious because of language or simple, agreed-upon facts.
The view that a dispute is caused by different meanings, so it is not a disagreement about the world itself.
The view that no answer to a question is true because there is no fact that settles it.
A disagreement about how a word or idea should be used, rather than about an independent fact.
A debate about whether something exists, such as tables, numbers, or objects from the past.

questions_to_think_about: How is asking whether tables exist different from asking whether the table question is a good question?
Can two people disagree about a sentence while agreeing about every ordinary fact?
What would count as evidence that an existence question has no fact of the matter?
Why might a philosopher think that one meaning of “exists” is better than another?
Can a criticism of metaphysics avoid becoming another philosophical theory?
